patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.setting: GP surgery, then endocrinology day unit
patient.complaint: Passing large volumes of urine and constant thirst for 4 months
background: Bipolar disorder, on lithium for 12 years, stable

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with polyuria, polydipsia and a normal glucose: lithium points to nephrogenic DI, head injury or pituitary disease to cranial DI.

points: Daniel, 46, sees his GP: **passing huge volumes of urine**.
Up 5 times a night; drinks water from the bathroom tap.
On **lithium for bipolar disorder** for 12 years.
Craves ice-cold water; no weight loss.

steps.lead: Daniel's kidneys cannot hold on to water, so he makes **large volumes of dilute urine** and drinks to keep up.

steps.q: Daniel's glucose is normal. Which type of DI does his history point to?
steps.r: Long-term **lithium** makes the collecting duct resistant to ADH: **nephrogenic** DI.

steps.lead: Daniel's 12 years of **lithium** is the classic cause of nephrogenic DI. Head injury, sarcoid, meningitis or a pituitary tumour would point to cranial DI.

steps.title: Polyuria: think in order
nodes: Check calcium and potassium → exclude hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia
Raised serum osmolality + dilute urine → suspect DI
Drug history (lithium) or head/pituitary insult → type
steps.caption: Diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause of polyuria, so rule it out first.

steps.lead: Daniel has **nocturia**, disturbed sleep and dilute urine. If he could not get to water, he would become dehydrated and **hypernatraemic**.

steps.text: Primary polydipsia also gives dilute urine, but the **serum sodium is low-normal** because the person is overloaded with water, not short of it.
In the exam, a patient on **lithium** with polyuria and a high sodium is nephrogenic DI. After head injury or pituitary surgery it is cranial DI.

investigation.exam: Expect 'initial' (paired serum and urine osmolality) versus 'diagnostic' (water deprivation test), and reading the result after desmopressin.

steps.lead: Daniel's first tests are **paired serum and urine osmolality**: a concentrated blood with a dilute urine raises the suspicion of DI.

steps.title: GP bloods and urine
steps.text: High serum osmolality with inappropriately dilute urine; glucose and calcium normal.

visual.title: Daniel's serum sodium
visual.label: Daniel 148
visual.caption: Mild hypernatraemia from water loss. Primary polydipsia would sit at the low end of normal.

steps.lead: To confirm it and find the type, Daniel has a **water deprivation test**, then desmopressin.

visual.title: Water deprivation test: urine osmolality
visual.caption: Daniel's urine stays **below 300** even after desmopressin: his kidneys ignore ADH, so this is **nephrogenic** DI.

steps.q: A patient with confirmed **cranial** DI and no head injury. Which test next?
steps.r: Cranial DI needs the hypothalamus and pituitary imaged to look for a tumour or infiltration.

steps.lead: Daniel's U&Es check his kidneys, which lithium also harms. Had his DI been **cranial**, an **MRI pituitary** would come next.

steps.text: Do not give desmopressin first and skip the deprivation phase. The **deprivation** shows the urine cannot concentrate; desmopressin then shows the type.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate treatment?': desmopressin for cranial DI, treat the cause then a thiazide for nephrogenic DI, never fluid restriction.

steps.lead: Daniel has nephrogenic DI, so desmopressin will not work. Treat the cause (**review lithium**), then a **thiazide** if polyuria persists.

steps.q: What is the most appropriate first step for Daniel's DI?
steps.r: Lithium is the cause, but stopping it abruptly risks relapse of bipolar disorder: change it **with psychiatry**.

steps.title: Treatment by type
nodes: Confirm type with water deprivation test
Nephrogenic DI → treat cause (stop or adjust lithium)
Everyone → drink to thirst, low-salt diet

steps.text: Thiazides **raise lithium levels**. If a thiazide is started while Daniel is still on lithium, his lithium level must be checked closely.

steps.lead: Daniel is told to keep water close by, drink to thirst and eat a **low-salt diet**, which cuts the solute load and so urine volume.

visual.title: Daniel's urine output
visual.caption: Lithium-induced DI may only partly recover; the thiazide cuts output further.

steps.lead: Daniel's care follows **NICE CKS** and **Society for Endocrinology** guidance: confirm the type, treat the cause, and use the right drug.

steps.text: Never fluid-restrict a patient with DI: they will become severely **hypernatraemic**. Fluid restriction is for SIADH, the opposite problem.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: where ADH acts, how lithium causes nephrogenic DI and why thiazides reduce urine output.

steps.lead: Daniel's posterior pituitary releases ADH normally, but his **collecting duct** cannot insert aquaporin-2 channels in response.

steps.title: How ADH concentrates urine
nodes: ADH binds V2 receptors in the collecting duct
steps.caption: Cranial DI breaks the first two steps; nephrogenic DI breaks the last three.

steps.lead: Lithium got into Daniel's principal cells through **ENaC** channels and built up there, switching down aquaporin-2.
Water pours out, so Daniel's plasma **osmolality and sodium rise**, which drives his thirst.
A thiazide makes Daniel mildly volume-depleted, so his **proximal tubule** reabsorbs more salt and water and less reaches the collecting duct.

steps.text: Desmopressin is a **V2 receptor agonist**: it replaces missing ADH in cranial DI but cannot help when the receptor pathway is broken.

mcq.q: What is the classic drug cause of nephrogenic DI?
mcq.r: Lithium accumulates in collecting duct cells.

mcq.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is typical of DI?
mcq.r: Free water loss concentrates the sodium.

mcq.q: Which is a cause of cranial DI?
mcq.r: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary.

mcq.q: What is the newer name for nephrogenic DI?
mcq.r: The kidney resists normal or high ADH.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard test for DI?
mcq.r: It confirms DI and, with desmopressin, the type.

mcq.q: In cranial DI, urine osmolality after desmopressin:
mcq.r: The kidney responds to the replaced ADH.

mcq.q: Which first-line pair raises suspicion of DI?
o: High serum and high urine osmolality
High serum and low urine osmolality
Low serum and high urine osmolality
Low serum and low urine osmolality
Mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal tubule
V1 receptors in the proximal tubule
V2 receptors in the collecting duct

prompts.q: What is diabetes insipidus and what are its two types?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the type from the cause.

points.p: Impaired renal water reabsorption: large volumes of dilute urine and polydipsia
Cranial DI (AVP deficiency): ADH production is faulty
Nephrogenic DI (AVP resistance): kidneys ignore ADH

prompts.q: What are the causes of cranial and nephrogenic DI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you the cause.

points.p: Cranial: head injury, pituitary tumour or surgery
Cranial: sarcoidosis, meningitis, sickle cell, idiopathic, genetic
Nephrogenic: lithium (classic)
Nephrogenic: chronic kidney disease

prompts.q: How does DI present, and what happens in severe cases?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity is about access to water.

points.p: Polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, disturbed sleep
Dilute urine with low osmolality
Severe: dehydration, hypernatraemia, hypotension

prompts.q: How do you tell DI from primary polydipsia and diabetes mellitus?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: sodium and glucose are the quick discriminators.

points.p: Diabetes mellitus: raised glucose
points.why: Commonest cause of polyuria; check first.

points.p: DI: sodium high-normal or high; primary polydipsia: low-normal
Primary polydipsia concentrates urine on water deprivation

prompts.q: What are the first-line and second-line tests for DI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what each test is for.

points.p: Serum and urine osmolality first
points.why: High serum, low urine = suspect DI.

points.p: U&Es
MRI pituitary for a cranial cause

prompts.q: How is the water deprivation test interpreted?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two phases, two questions.

points.p: It is the gold-standard confirmatory test
Cranial DI: dilute during deprivation, rises above 305 mOsm/kg after desmopressin
Nephrogenic DI: stays below 300 mOsm/kg even after desmopressin

prompts.q: How is each type of DI treated?

points.p: Cranial: intranasal desmopressin
Nephrogenic: treat the cause, e.g. stop or adjust lithium
Nephrogenic first-line drug: thiazide diuretic
Long term: low-salt diet and adequate fluid intake

prompts.q: How does ADH normally work, and how does each type fail?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: follow the hormone from brain to duct.

points.p: Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary
Acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2
Lithium enters via ENaC and downregulates aquaporin-2
Loss of ADH action: dilute urine, rising plasma osmolality and sodium, thirst

prompts.q: Why do thiazides reduce urine output in nephrogenic DI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: it happens upstream of the collecting duct.

points.p: Mild volume depletion
Increased proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption
points.why: Less fluid reaches the collecting duct.

glossary.diabetes insipidus: Passing large volumes of dilute urine because ADH is lacking or the kidneys ignore it.
glossary.cranial DI: DI from too little ADH made or released by the hypothalamus or pituitary.
glossary.nephrogenic DI: DI because the kidney does not respond to ADH.
glossary.ADH: Antidiuretic hormone: makes the kidney reabsorb water and concentrate urine.
glossary.AVP: Arginine vasopressin, another name for ADH.
glossary.desmopressin: Synthetic ADH analogue that acts on V2 receptors; treats cranial DI.
glossary.V2 receptor: ADH receptor in the collecting duct that triggers aquaporin-2 insertion.
glossary.aquaporin-2: Water channel inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
glossary.collecting duct: Final part of the nephron, where ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed.
glossary.principal cells: Collecting duct cells that respond to ADH and aldosterone.
glossary.ENaC: Epithelial sodium channel; lithium enters collecting duct cells through it.
glossary.posterior pituitary: Back lobe of the pituitary that stores and releases ADH.
glossary.hypothalamus: Brain region that makes ADH and senses plasma osmolality.
glossary.osmolality: Concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid, measured in mOsm/kg.
glossary.polyuria: Passing abnormally large volumes of urine, often over 3 L a day.
glossary.nocturia: Waking at night to pass urine.
glossary.primary polydipsia: Drinking too much water, often psychiatric; urine is dilute but sodium is low-normal.
glossary.water deprivation test: Withholds fluid, then gives desmopressin, to confirm DI and its type.
glossary.lithium: Mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder; the classic cause of nephrogenic DI.
glossary.thiazide: Diuretic acting on the distal tubule; paradoxically reduces urine in nephrogenic DI.
glossary.bendroflumethiazide: A commonly used thiazide diuretic in the UK.
glossary.sarcoidosis: Inflammatory disease with granulomas that can infiltrate the pituitary and hypothalamus.
glossary.SIADH: Too much ADH: low sodium and concentrated urine, the opposite of DI.
glossary.tolvaptan: V2 receptor antagonist that blocks ADH; used for SIADH, not DI.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes blood test, including sodium and creatinine.
glossary.transsphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery through the nose; a common cause of cranial DI.
glossary.proximal tubule: First part of the nephron, which reabsorbs most filtered salt and water.
glossary.bipolar disorder: Mood disorder with episodes of mania and depression; often treated with lithium.

technique.stem: A 28 year old man has passed large volumes of urine and been extremely thirsty since he was knocked off his bike 2 weeks ago and hit his head. He drinks 8 L of water a day. His BP is 116/72 mmHg and pulse rate 96 bpm. His capillary glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about polyuria: exclude diabetes mellitus, then pick the type of DI.
Polyuria and polydipsia after **head injury** with a normal glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary: **cranial DI**.

elim: Glucose is normal.
No lithium, CKD or kidney cause; the trigger is a head injury.
The thirst began abruptly after trauma; no psychiatric history.
Causes low sodium and concentrated urine with no polyuria.

steps.x: **A. Cranial diabetes insipidus.** Head injury + polyuria + normal glucose = cranial DI.

technique.stem: A 39 year old woman has 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia. Her serum sodium is 147 mmol/L, serum osmolality 301 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 160 mOsm/kg. Her glucose and calcium are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic investigation' means the gold-standard confirmatory test.
High serum osmolality with dilute urine; common causes of polyuria excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Water deprivation test** with desmopressin.

elim: Measures volume but does not show why the urine is dilute.
Done after cranial DI is confirmed, to find the cause.
Glucose is already normal.
She is not on lithium.

steps.x: **E. Water deprivation test.** DI is confirmed and typed by water deprivation then desmopressin.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman had transsphenoidal surgery for a pituitary macroadenoma 3 days ago. She is now passing 6 L of urine a day. Her serum sodium is 149 mmol/L. A water deprivation test confirms cranial diabetes insipidus.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

steps.x: Treatment of a confirmed type.
Cranial DI after pituitary surgery: she cannot make ADH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Replace it: **desmopressin** (V2 agonist).

elim: First-line for nephrogenic, not cranial, DI.
Would worsen her hypernatraemia; that is SIADH treatment.
Replaces cortisol; does not treat ADH deficiency.
A V2 antagonist that blocks ADH: the opposite of what she needs.

steps.x: **D. Intranasal desmopressin.** Cranial DI → desmopressin; nephrogenic DI → treat cause, then thiazide.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 15 years. He has polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 mmol/L. His urine osmolality stays below 300 mOsm/kg after desmopressin.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his polyuria?
o: Downregulation of aquaporin-2 in collecting duct cells
Reduced ADH synthesis in the hypothalamus

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain why the kidney ignores ADH.
Long-term lithium and no response to desmopressin: **nephrogenic DI**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lithium enters principal cells via ENaC and **downregulates aquaporin-2**.

elim: That is cranial DI; he would respond to desmopressin.
Causes hypertension and low K+, not ADH resistance.
Glucose is not the problem here.
Cranial DI again; desmopressin would work.

steps.x: **B. Downregulation of aquaporin-2 in collecting duct cells.** Lithium → ENaC → accumulates → less aquaporin-2 → ADH resistance.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman with bipolar disorder has a 6 month history of passing large amounts of urine and waking at night to drink. She has taken lithium for 10 years. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Lithium is the classic cause of nephrogenic DI. Primary polydipsia gives a low-normal sodium, and hypothyroidism does not cause polyuria.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: polyuria plus a drug history.
Long-term **lithium**, nocturia, high sodium and normal glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nephrogenic DI**.

elim: No head injury, surgery or pituitary cause; lithium points to the kidney.
Glucose is normal.
Lithium can cause it, but it does not cause polyuria.
Sodium is high, not low-normal.

steps.x: **D. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.** Lithium + polyuria + high sodium = nephrogenic DI.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman had breast cancer treated 4 years ago. She has a 1 month history of headaches, extreme thirst and passing urine every hour. Her BP is 128/78 mmHg and pulse rate 90 bpm. Her glucose and calcium are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Breast cancer can metastasise to the pituitary, causing cranial DI. Hypercalcaemia is excluded by the normal calcium.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: polyuria in someone with past cancer.
Headache plus new polyuria: a deposit in the **pituitary or hypothalamus**. Calcium and glucose normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cranial DI** from a metastasis to the pituitary stalk.

elim: Calcium is normal.
No lithium or renal disease; headache points to the brain.
No psychiatric history; new headache suggests a structural cause.
Causes low sodium without polyuria.

steps.x: **A. Cranial diabetes insipidus.** Cancer + headache + polyuria with normal calcium = cranial DI.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has a 2 month history of polyuria and polydipsia. He has no past medical history. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Blood and urine tests are sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely pair of results?
practice.e: In DI water is lost in dilute urine, so serum osmolality rises while urine osmolality stays inappropriately low.

steps.x: A 'most likely result' question: predict the biochemistry of DI.
Polyuria and polydipsia in a well man: think DI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High serum osmolality with inappropriately low urine osmolality**.

elim: Low serum with dilute urine is primary polydipsia.
Low serum with concentrated urine is SIADH.
Normal, appropriately concentrated urine.
Appropriate concentration: the kidneys are holding water, as in dehydration.

steps.x: **D. Serum osmolality 304, urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg.** DI = concentrated blood, dilute urine.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has a dry cough, tender red lumps on his shins and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. He has developed polyuria and a water deprivation test confirms cranial diabetes insipidus. His BP is 124/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his diabetes insipidus?
practice.e: Sarcoidosis can infiltrate the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk, causing cranial DI with hypernatraemia.

steps.x: A cause question: the DI type is given, find the disease behind it.

clues: tender red lumps on his shins
steps.x: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and dry cough: **sarcoidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neurosarcoid infiltrating the hypothalamus/pituitary causes **cranial DI**.

elim: Causes nephrogenic, not cranial, DI; no lithium given.
No fever, neck stiffness or acute illness.
A cause of cranial DI in the notes, but nothing in the stem suggests it.
Can cause hilar nodes, but erythema nodosum with bilateral hilar nodes is classic sarcoid.

steps.x: **C. Sarcoidosis.** Sarcoid is an inflammatory cause of cranial DI and tends to cause hypernatraemia.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman on long-term lithium has polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 mmol/L. She has a water deprivation test followed by desmopressin.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result?
o: Urine osmolality rises above 800 mOsm/kg at 4 hours
Urine stays dilute throughout, even after desmopressin
practice.e: In nephrogenic DI the collecting duct ignores both endogenous and exogenous ADH, so urine stays below 300 mOsm/kg.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question on a test result.
Lithium + hypernatraemia = **nephrogenic DI**: the kidney ignores ADH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No response to deprivation **or** desmopressin: urine stays below 300 mOsm/kg.

elim: That is normal or primary polydipsia.
That is cranial DI.
Normal concentrating ability.
Desmopressin reduces volume when it works; it does not increase it.

steps.x: **D. Urine stays dilute throughout, even after desmopressin.** Nephrogenic DI: dilute throughout. Cranial DI: concentrates only after desmopressin.

practice.stem: An 82 year old woman with known cranial diabetes insipidus is brought from her care home after 2 days of a chest infection. She has been too drowsy to drink. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bibasal fine crackles from fluid overload
practice.e: Unable to drink, she cannot replace dilute urine losses, so she becomes dehydrated, hypernatraemic and hypotensive.

steps.x: An examination finding question.
DI with **no access to water**: free water loss goes unreplaced.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe dehydration and **hypernatraemia** with hypotension: **dry mucous membranes**.

elim: She is water-depleted, not overloaded.
Implies overload, not free water loss.
Her intravascular volume is low.
Hypovolaemia gives cool peripheries.

steps.x: **B. Dry mucous membranes.** DI + cannot drink = dehydration, hypernatraemia, hypotension.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has 6 weeks of polyuria and polydipsia. Her capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She takes no medication.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: High serum with inappropriately low urine osmolality raises suspicion of DI before the water deprivation test.

steps.x: 'Initial' means the first-line test.
Polyuria with normal glucose: next ask whether this is DI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Serum and urine osmolality** together.

elim: Treating before confirming risks dangerous hyponatraemia if she has primary polydipsia.
Only once cranial DI is confirmed.
Does not assess concentrating ability.
The gold standard, but done after first-line osmolalities raise suspicion.

steps.x: **C. Paired serum and urine osmolality.** First-line = paired osmolalities; confirm = water deprivation test.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has polyuria. A water deprivation test shows dilute urine during deprivation, with urine osmolality rising to 680 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. He has no history of head injury. His BP is 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Cranial DI needs MRI pituitary to look for a tumour or infiltration of the hypothalamus or stalk.

steps.x: 'Next' investigation after the diagnosis is made.
Concentrates only after desmopressin: **cranial DI**. No obvious cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Image the hypothalamus and pituitary: **MRI pituitary**.

elim: The kidney responded to desmopressin; the problem is central.
The result is already diagnostic.
Lithium causes nephrogenic DI; he responded to desmopressin.
Tests adrenal reserve; not the next step for the cause.

steps.x: **B. MRI pituitary.** Cranial DI without a clear cause → MRI pituitary.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man with bipolar disorder well controlled on lithium for 14 years has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus confirmed on water deprivation testing. His serum sodium is 147 mmol/L. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop lithium immediately and start no alternative
practice.e: Treating the cause comes first; lithium should be changed in liaison with psychiatry, not stopped abruptly.

steps.x: Next step in management of a known cause.
Nephrogenic DI from lithium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the cause: **stop or adjust lithium** with psychiatry.

elim: Would worsen hypernatraemia.
Does not work: the kidney ignores ADH.
Risks a bipolar relapse.
Blocks ADH and would worsen water loss.

steps.x: **C. Review lithium with his psychiatrist.** Nephrogenic DI → remove the cause first, safely.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman stopped lithium 6 months ago because of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. She still passes 5 L of urine a day. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
practice.e: Thiazides cause mild volume depletion, increasing proximal reabsorption and reducing collecting duct flow.

steps.x: Drug treatment after the cause is removed.
Persistent nephrogenic DI despite stopping lithium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line drug: **thiazide diuretic**, which paradoxically reduces urine output.

elim: Ineffective in nephrogenic DI.
A loop diuretic increases dilute urine loss.
No cortisol deficiency.
Does not reduce collecting duct water delivery in this way.

steps.x: **E. Thiazide diuretic.** Nephrogenic DI drug = thiazide.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has idiopathic nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. He takes a thiazide diuretic. He asks what else he can do. His BP is 118/72 mmHg and serum sodium 145 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Fluid restriction to 1 L a day
Low-salt diet with drinking to thirst
practice.e: A low-salt diet reduces solute load and so urine volume; fluid must never be restricted in DI.

steps.x: Long-term advice question.
Established nephrogenic DI on treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low-salt diet** and adequate fluid intake.

elim: Dangerous in DI: rapid hypernatraemia.
Increases solute load and urine volume.
Increases solute load and urine output.
Thirst is protective; the thiazide reduces output.

steps.x: **D. Low-salt diet with drinking to thirst.** DI long-term: low salt, never restrict fluid.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus starts bendroflumethiazide. Her 24-hour urine volume falls from 7 L to 4 L. Her BP is 116/70 mmHg and pulse rate 82 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in urine volume?
o: Increased ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Increased proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption
Inhibition of the loop of Henle
practice.e: Thiazide-induced volume depletion increases proximal sodium and water reabsorption, so less fluid reaches the collecting duct.

steps.x: A mechanism question about a paradox.
A diuretic reducing urine output in nephrogenic DI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild volume depletion → **more proximal reabsorption** → less fluid reaches the collecting duct.

elim: Her kidney ignores ADH regardless.
The ADH pathway stays broken.
That is a loop diuretic's action and would increase urine.
Glucose is not involved.

steps.x: **C. Increased proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption.** Thiazide paradox = volume depletion drives proximal reabsorption.
